title: Facts (Non-Negotiable), Conclusions (Negotiable)
author: John Mark Reynolds
summary: John Mark Reynolds takes on the popular demand that schools teach only neutral facts and practical skills. His central claim is that this demand quietly assumes a philosophy, because deciding which facts, which parts of the past and which skills count as basic already depends on values. He argues that facts are the raw data for good conclusions but cannot by themselves supply an ought, so an education built only on job skills makes a philosophic choice that is hard to defend. He extends the point to curriculum, classroom design and even screens, showing that avoiding value-laden questions is itself a way of teaching a value. Experts cannot settle the matter either, since they share the assumptions of their own guild. He concludes that a society short on shared values must extend mercy and good faith to its neighbors while negotiating what is true, good and beautiful enough to teach.
points: The demand for a neutral, facts-only education is itself a philosophy, because choosing what counts as basic or practical always rests on a view of what is most important.
Education aimed only at job skills without wisdom is a philosophic choice, which pushes the classical question of what makes a civilized, educated person back to the center.
Even a simple science lesson raises value-laden questions, so avoiding them is itself teaching a value by omission.
Appeals to experts do not end the debate, because experts share guild assumptions that can harden into a monoculture.
Reynolds frames the way forward as trust, good faith and mercy among people who disagree about conclusions while still treating facts as non-negotiable.
quotes: There is great value in knowing facts. They are the data needed for good conclusions. Practical skills are called practical for a reason!
Yet there is a simple problem with this demand: it assumes a philosophy! Can one consistently pry apart “facts” from “values?
Hours a day spent learning “job skills” without wisdom is a philosophic choice, but one that is hard to defend. What makes a civilized, educated person?
An inconvenient fact is that we do not all agree about the basics. Why? Our philosophy informs what seems basic to us!

Even the simplest discussion of a scientific fact can lead a student to ask a value-laden question. “Why should we wear or not wear masks?” If we avoid those questions, we are teaching a value by doing so.
Every perspective cannot be taught. Some assumptions will prevail if there is any coherence to an education at all.
Facts are not negotiable, but mercy on each other as we find a common good, truth, and beauty to teach can be, must be, negotiated.
